Myths · 27 November 2026

Do opposites attract?

It is a favourite of films and songs, but research on attraction and couples nearly always points the other way.

"They're like oil and water, that's why they complement each other." The idea that opposites attract has an obvious charm: it promises that each of us will find someone who has what we lack. But when it is studied with data, the picture is almost the reverse.

What the studies show

In the 1960s and 1970s, Donn Byrne designed a series of simple experiments. He gave participants an attitude questionnaire supposedly filled in by a stranger and asked how much they thought they would like that person. The more the stranger's attitudes matched their own, the more attractive the stranger seemed. Byrne called this regularity the attraction paradigm, and it has been replicated many times.

Something similar happens outside the lab. Couples tend to resemble each other in age, education, values, religion, politics and even habits such as smoking. Researchers call this assortative mating.

What about complementarity?

In 1958 the sociologist Robert Winch argued that we choose partners for complementary needs: a dominant person would look for someone more submissive, for example. It was an influential hypothesis, but later studies did not support it consistently.

A 2008 meta-analysis by Matthew Montoya and colleagues pooled more than three hundred studies. It concluded that similarity is linked to attraction, especially early on. It added an interesting nuance: in established relationships, perceived similarity matters more than actual similarity. Believing we are alike also brings people together.

Why the myth survives

Partly because contrasts catch the eye and are easier to remember. Partly because some differences do work: two people can split tasks according to what each is better at, and that feels like complementing each other. But these are usually differences set against a shared background of values and expectations.

The takeaway

Being alike guarantees nothing, and being different does not doom a relationship. What research on couples tends to highlight is less eye-catching: how disagreements are talked through, how much attention goes into everyday life, and whether both feel they are pulling in the same direction.

References

  1. Byrne, D. (1971). The Attraction Paradigm. Nueva York: Academic Press.
  2. Winch, R. F. (1958). Mate-Selection: A Study of Complementary Needs. Nueva York: Harper.
  3. Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S. y Kirchner, J. (2008). Is actual similarity necessary for attraction? A meta-analysis of actual and perceived similarity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 25(6), 889–922.
  4. Luo, S. y Klohnen, E. C. (2005). Assortative mating and marital quality in newlyweds: A couple-centered approach. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 88(2), 304–326.
